t.6.89.2: This heroic Lakṣmaṇa, struck down to the earth by the force of Rāvaṇa, writhes like a serpent, stirring up my grief.
t.6.89.1: Having waged a tumultuous battle against the evil-minded Rāvaṇa, he, even while still loosing floods of arrows, spoke these words to Suṣeṇa.
t.6.89.3: As I behold this hero, dearer to me than my very life, drenched in blood, what power have I to fight, my mind utterly distraught?
t.6.89.4: This is my brother, who glories in battle and bears auspicious marks; if he has gone to death, what use to me is life, or what use is happiness?
t.6.89.5: My valor seems to shrink in shame, and the bow seems to slip from my hand; my arrows sink down, and my sight is overcome by tears. A fierce anxiety grows within me, and a longing for death arises.
t.6.89.6: Seeing his brother struck down by the evil-minded Rāvaṇa, he fell into the deepest despair and, his senses in turmoil, lamented.
t.6.89.7: Having seen my brother Lakṣmaṇa struck down in the dust of the battlefield, I have no use for battle, none at all for my life, nor for Sītā.
t.6.89.8: What use is kingship to me, what use is life? There is nothing left for me to do in battle, now that Lakṣmaṇa lies here slain at the forefront of the fight.
t.6.89.9: Consoling Rāma, the heroic Suṣeṇa spoke these words: "This mighty-armed Lakṣmaṇa, the increaser of fortune, is not dead."
t.6.89.10: His face is not distorted, nor darkened, nor lacking in lustre; his countenance is seen to be radiant and serene.
t.6.89.11: His hands have palms red as lotuses, and his eyes are quite clear; such an appearance is not found in those whose life has departed, O lord of the people. Do not give way to despair, O hero; he still has his breath, O subduer of foes.
t.6.89.12: O hero, the heart of him who lies asleep on the ground with slackened limbs, still breathing and trembling again and again, will tell the truth of it.
t.6.89.13: Having thus spoken these words to Rāghava, Suṣeṇa, skilled in speech, hastily said this to Hanūmān, who stood nearby.
t.6.89.14: O gentle one, go quickly from here to the mountain, the Herb Mountain, that auspicious one, O hero, which was described to you earlier by Jāmbavān.
t.6.89.15: Bring the auspicious herb that grows on its southern peak, the one named Viśalyakaraṇī, which draws out the arrows and heals the wounded.
t.6.89.16: Go quickly and bring here the sauvarṇakaraṇī, and likewise the saṃjīvanī, and also the saṃdhānakaraṇī, for the reviving of the heroic, great-souled Lakṣmaṇa.
t.6.89.17: Thus addressed, the glorious Hanumān went to the mountain of herbs, and, not knowing those great medicinal herbs, he fell into deep thought.
t.6.89.18: A thought arose in the mind of Māruti, of immeasurable might: "Seizing this very peak of the mountain, I shall go."
t.6.89.19: If I go back without taking the viśalyakaraṇī herb, the loss of time would be a fault, and great distress would arise.
t.6.89.20: Having thus reflected, the mighty Hanumān went swiftly, and Hanumān, seizing the peak of the mountain, leapt up into the air.
t.6.89.21: I could not recognize those herbs, O bull among monkeys; therefore I have brought this entire peak of that mountain.
t.6.89.22: Praising the son of the Wind-god as he spoke thus, Suṣeṇa, the foremost of the monkeys, uprooted the herbs and took them.
t.6.89.23: Then Suṣeṇa, the foremost of monkeys, of exceedingly great splendor, crushed that herb and gave it to Lakṣmaṇa through the nose.
t.6.89.25: Seeing Lakṣmaṇa risen up from the ground, those monkeys, greatly delighted, honored Suṣeṇa, crying, "Well done, well done!"
t.6.89.24: Lakṣmaṇa, slayer of enemy heroes, still pierced by the arrow, smelled it and swiftly rose from the ground, freed of the arrow and free of pain.
t.6.89.26: Rāma, the slayer of enemy heroes, said to Lakṣmaṇa, "Come, come!" and, his eyes clouded with tears, embraced him tightly with deep affection.
t.6.89.28: I have no use for life, nor for Sītā, nor for victory. Indeed, what use is life to me when you have returned to the five elements?
t.6.89.27: Then Rāghava, embracing Saumitri, said: "By good fortune, O hero, I see you come back again from death."
t.6.89.29: While the great-souled Rāghava was speaking thus, Lakṣmaṇa, exhausted, spoke these words in a faltering voice.
t.6.89.30: O you of true valor, having formerly made that solemn vow, you ought not to speak thus here, like some trifling man devoid of courage.
t.6.89.31: O sinless one, the virtuous never let a promise prove false, for the keeping of one's promise is the great mark of such a man.
t.6.89.32: Enough, then, of giving way to despair on my account, O sinless one; fulfil your vow today by slaying Rāvaṇa.
t.6.89.33: Your enemy, having come into the path of your arrows, will not escape alive, just as a great elephant will not escape from a roaring, sharp-fanged lion.
t.6.89.34: But I desire the swift slaying of this evil-minded one, before this sun, its work accomplished, goes to its setting.
